title: Harmony Through Numbers: Classifying Spotify Data Across Genres and Decades
text: Through this project, our group sought to bridge the gap between music and data science by employing Spotify’s extensive datasets to perform assorted classification tasks. Using various metrics provided by Spotify, such as danceability, energy, and loudness, we aimed to categorize music into genres and decades. Our goal was to implement sophisticated data analysis techniques learned in class to perform classification at both the artist and track levels. This project explores the feasibility of such classifications and tests the effectiveness of different machine-learning models in handling uniquely complex data, such as music. By applying these methods, we aim to deepen our understanding of musical trends and patterns, enhancing our ability to predict and categorize musical genres more effectively. Furthermore, this study is a practical example of how data science can be applied in creative industries, demonstrating the potential for machine learning to influence and innovate within the music sector.

title: Harmony Through Numbers: Classifying Spotify Data Across Genres and Decades
text:
Artist Level Genre Classification

Data Setup
In the initial steps of our project, we utilized essential Python libraries, such as numpy and pandas, which are crucial for numerical operations and data manipulation. We loaded our primary dataset, artists.csv, into a pandas DataFrame. This dataset contains detailed information about music artists, including their names and associated genres. An immediate examination of the dataset provided an understanding of its structure, which includes various columns critical to our analysis.


Data Exploration and Cleansing
During our data exploration phase, we identified rows where the genre information was missing key data for our genre classification model. Specific corrections included rectifying genre assignments for artists like “The Beach Boys” and removing entries with corrupted data, such as “Roger Miller.” This cleansing step ensured the accuracy and reliability of our dataset, setting a solid foundation for further analysis and modeling.


Assigning a Primary Genre
As musicians can belong to numerous genres, we initially investigated performing multi-label, multi-class classification. This effort proved ineffective with such a small dataset of approximately 400 artists. Next, we assigned a primary genre for each artist and perform single-label, multi-class classification. To do this, we first removed four of the ten genres: pop, rap, jazz, and funk. These genres were chosen for a combination of two reasons: cannibalization with other genres and lacking a specific genre identity. We were then left with six distinct genres: country, EDM, hip-hop, Latin, rock, and soul. While we had removed much of the cannibalization, numerous artists still had more than one Spotify-assigned genre. To address this issue, we used the Spotify rankings within each genre. We created a function capable of comparing their rank across genres in hopes of determining what genre an artist was more important to. These comparisons allowed us to assign a primary genre for each artist in our dataset, leaving us with about 300 artists while ensuring that our classifications are accurate. This comprehensive approach to data preparation prepared our dataset for effective machine learning applications.


Machine Learning Preparation
We prepared our dataset for machine learning by splitting it into training and test sets, which is a standard practice for evaluating a model’s performance on unseen data. We also converted categorical variables into numerical format using techniques such as one-hot encoding. These transformations are crucial for training machine learning models that require numerical input, setting the stage for robust model training.


Model Training and Evaluation
In this section of our project, we evaluated several machine learning models to determine the most effective approach for classifying music genres based on artist data. Each model was assessed based upon its accuracy and computation time, which are crucial factors in practical applications. Below is a summary of the outcomes for each model:

Logistic Regression

Test Accuracy: 81.03%
Computation Time: 3.2 seconds
Comments: Logistic Regression provided a robust balance between speed and accuracy, proving to be highly efficient for scenarios where prompt results are necessary without significantly compromising performance.



Support Vector Machine (SVM)

Test Accuracy: 77.59%
Computation Time: 3.4 seconds
Comments: SVM displayed slightly lower accuracy compared to Logistic Regression and had a comparable speed. It is generally well-suited for linearly separable data, but showed moderate performance in our multi-class classification task.



Neural Network

Train Accuracy: 68.85%
Test Accuracy: 70.69%
Computation Time: 11 minutes 46.2 seconds
Comments: The Neural Network required considerably more training time and yielded lower accuracy even with adjusted hyperparameters. Despite their capabilities, neural networks generally require a lot of data to learn effectively and might overfit or underperform on smaller datasets where simpler models may be more effective.



Random Forest

Test Accuracy: 79.31%
Computation Time: 1 minute 6.4 seconds
Comments: Random Forest achieved good accuracy, suggesting effective handling of the diverse and feature-rich data through its ensemble method. The computational time was reasonable for an ensemble approach, making it a strong contender.



XGBoost

Test Accuracy: 77.59%
Computation Time: 24.5 seconds
Comments: XGBoost is well known for its high performance in structured data problems. Here, it offered competitive accuracy with SVM but required longer training time. Its efficient management of various data structures makes it a valuable model despite the higher computational cost.




Hyperparameter Tuning
We implemented grid searches to fine tune each model’s hyperparameters and optimize its performance. This step was crucial in identifying the most effective model settings for our specific dataset and artist-based genre classification task. With the chosen hyperparameters, the models were evaluated on the test set to determine how they perform on unseen data. These results provided a definitive assessment of our model’s performance and its ability to generalize on new data.


Conclusion: Classifying Artists into Genres
The genre classification at the artist level proved to be quite successful, routinely achieving test accuracies over 75%, with logistic regression peaking at 81%. This classification was significantly higher than a baseline model of random guessing, indicative of the effectiveness of our feature selection and machine learning techniques.

title: Harmony Through Numbers: Classifying Spotify Data Across Genres and Decades
text:
Track Level Genre Classification

Data Setup
We imported necessary Python libraries such as numpy and pandas, essential for handling large datasets and numerical computations. The primary dataset, tracks.csv, was loaded into a pandas DataFrame. This dataset contains detailed attributes of music tracks such as danceability, energy, loudness, and other features that describe the audio characteristics of the tracks.


Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
Initial data cleaning involved handling missing values, especially in the genre column, which is crucial for our classification task. We also discarded any irrelevant or redundant data points to avoid skewing our results and impairing our models’ efficiency. This cleaning step ensured a more focused and efficient dataset ready for the subsequent stages of our analysis.


Integration and Processing of Genre-Specific Data
By integrating genre_of_artists.csv with our track data, we linked each track with its corresponding artist’s genre, thereby enriching our dataset with essential classification labels. This integration streamlined the data and enriched it, providing a solid foundation for accurate genre classification. We decided to use this approach since we were unable to acquire genre information for individual tracks.


Feature Engineering and Data Integration
We conducted feature engineering as well, which included encoding categorical variables, normalizing numerical values, and creating new features that could provide more insights into the genre classification. Features derived from the key_mode column, such as musical key and mode, were particularly significant, as these musical aspects are often strong indicators of genre.


Machine Learning Preparation
The prepared dataset was split into training and test sets to validate the effectiveness of the models. This step is critical in assessing how well our model performs on new, unseen data and ensuring that we accurately gauge its real world applicability.


Model Training and Evaluation
We trained and evaluated several machine learning models to classify tracks into genres. Each model’s performance was assessed based on accuracy and computation time. Below is a summary of how each model performed:

Logistic Regression

Test Accuracy: 51.38%
Computation Time: 6 minutes 3.89 seconds



Support Vector Machine (SVM)

Test Accuracy: 54.89%
Computation Time: 80 minutes 4.4 seconds



Neural Network

Train Accuracy: 54.45%
Test Accuracy: 49.18%
Computation Time: 44 minutes



Random Forest

Test Accuracy: 61.68%
Computation Time: 46 minutes 49.8 seconds



XGBoost

Test Accuracy: 63.03%
Computation Time: 2 minutes 51.4 seconds




Hyperparameter Tuning
We performed hyperparameter tuning using techniques such GridSearchCV to optimize each model’s performance. This process involved systematically testing different combinations of parameters to find the best setup for each model. The tuning was particularly crucial for complex models like Neural Networks and XGBoost, where the right combination of parameters can significantly impact the model’s effectiveness and efficiency.


Conclusion: Classifying Tracks into Genres
The track-level genre classification performed less optimally due to the inherent variability in songs by the same artist, peaking at 63% accuracy with XGBoost. This suggests that while machine learning can significantly aid in genre classification, the complex nature of music genres often requires more sophisticated models or multi-modal data integration to improve accuracy.

Project Overview

Twenty years after its Broadway debut, Wicked remains a streaming phenomenon. But what separates the most-played tracks from the forgotten ones? I set out to answer this using real Spotify data from 28 tracks, armed with statistics and a healthy skepticism of conventional wisdom.
Spoiler alert: Almost everything the music industry tells you about “successful songs” is backwards.
Using correlation analysis, ANOVA, K-means clustering, and PCA, I analyzed actual Spotify metrics to understand what makes certain songs resonate. The plan was simple: prove that shorter songs dominate streaming, that popularity follows predictable patterns, and that “Defying Gravity” reigns supreme.
Reality had other plans.
Turns out “For Good” wins, duration doesn’t matter even slightly (r=0.05, p=0.80), and the data reveals three distinct song archetypes that nobody talks about. Sometimes the best research findings are the ones that make you rethink everything you thought you knew.

What The Data Actually Showed

The Winner Nobody Expected (Sorry, Elphaba)
“For Good,” the emotional duet near the finale, scores highest in Spotify popularity (58/100), edging out crowd favorites like “Defying Gravity” (56) and “No Good Deed” (57). Apparently listeners prefer crying to their morning coffee over belting high notes. Who knew?


Duration Doesn’t Matter (And I Have Receipts)
Correlation between song length and popularity? A measly r=0.05 with p=0.80. Translation: whether a song runs 50 seconds or 7.6 minutes has zero predictive power for streaming success. ANOVA confirms it (F=1.76, p=0.19). The “keep it short for attention spans” advice? Statistically baseless-at least for this soundtrack.


Three Song Archetypes Nobody Talks About
K-means clustering (k=3) reveals distinct groups: Epic Numbers (long, popular showstoppers), Deep Cuts (short, less-streamed but plot-essential tracks), and Solid Mid-Tier (balanced popularity and length). It’s not a hierarchy. Each serves a different purpose. The soundtrack works because it has variety, not despite it.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
Lessons Learned (Besides Humility)

Technical Takeaways
API Wrangling: Spotify’s Web API is well-documented but temperamental. Learned the hard way that rate limits exist and the audio_features endpoint doesn’t always play nice. Solution: patience, retry logic, and strategic data collection.
Feature Engineering: Turned raw audio metrics into meaningful predictors. Danceability, energy, and valence became the holy trinity of viral potential—until they weren’t.
Machine Learning Reality Check: Random Forest models are excellent at finding patterns. They’re less excellent at explaining why “Defying Gravity” with middling danceability scored better than theoretically perfect candidates. Sometimes the model shrugs, and that’s data science.
Visualization Strategy: Interactive Plotly charts beat static images every time. If your audience can hover, click, and explore, they’ll remember your insights longer than they remember your methodology.


The Real Insight
Data science can tell you what happened. It can even tell you how it happened. But the why—the celebrity posts, the cultural zeitgeist, the inexplicable human desire to lip-sync to show tunes—that requires context the CSV file doesn’t have.
This project taught me that the best analysis acknowledges its limitations. The algorithm got us 85% of the way there. The other 15%? That’s where the interesting story lives.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
Methodology: Data Collection & Analysis


Python 3.11 Spotify API Pandas SciPy Scikit-learn Plotly

I collected data on 28 tracks from the Wicked soundtrack using Spotify’s Web API, capturing track metadata (name, duration, popularity scores) and analyzing patterns in listener engagement. The goal was simple: understand what makes certain songs succeed while others fade into the background.
The approach: descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, hypothesis testing (ANOVA, t-tests), unsupervised learning (K-means clustering, PCA), and interactive visualizations. No simulated data, no assumptions. Just real numbers from real listeners.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
The Numbers Tell a Story

Top 10 Songs by Spotify Popularity


        
        
        


                            
                                            



Observation: “For Good” takes the crown with a popularity score of 58, despite being one of the soundtrack’s longer tracks at 5.11 minutes. The emotional ballad outperforms even the showstopping “Defying Gravity” (56).
What this challenges: The assumption that “big, loud finales” are always the most popular. Sometimes the heartfelt conversation between two friends hits harder than the woman flying away on a broomstick. Data: 1, Conventional Wisdom: 0.
Bottom Line: The quiet moments win. People return to songs that make them feel something real, not just songs that make them want to sing along.



Duration vs. Popularity: The Surprising Non-Relationship


                            
                                            



Statistical Reality Check: With a correlation coefficient of just r=0.05 and p=0.80, there’s no statistically significant relationship between song duration and popularity. Duration explains less than 0.3% of variance in popularity (r²=0.0025).
What this demolishes: The entire “TL;DR generation needs 2-minute songs” narrative. “Dancing Through Life” clocks in at 7.62 minutes and sits comfortably in the top 10. Long-form content wins when it’s actually good. Revolutionary concept, I know.
Bottom Line: Song length doesn’t matter. If people love it, they’ll listen to all 7 minutes. If they don’t, they’ll skip it at 30 seconds. Quality > runtime.



K-Means Clustering: Three Song Archetypes


                            
                                            



Cluster Insight: K-means analysis (k=3) reveals three distinct song types that actually make sense:

Cluster 0: Epic Showstoppers - Long (avg 6.18 min), popular (avg 50.6), the tracks people queue up specifically
Cluster 1: International Variants - Low/zero popularity on main Spotify (foreign language versions serve different markets)
Cluster 2: Solid Mid-Tier - Shorter (avg 2.69 min), balanced popularity (avg 47.9), the narrative glue holding it all together

What this reveals: Successful soundtracks aren’t monoliths. They need peaks and valleys. The “filler tracks” aren’t filler-they’re structural. Remove them and the whole thing collapses. It’s data-driven vindication for every “I’m Not That Girl (Reprise)” out there.
Bottom Line: Great albums need variety. You can’t have all bangers-the quiet moments make the big moments matter. The “boring” tracks aren’t mistakes; they’re part of the design.



PCA Visualization: The Hidden Structure


                            
                                            



PCA Interpretation: Principal Component Analysis reduces our duration-popularity feature space to 2D while retaining 100% of the variance. PC1 (x-axis) captures combined magnitude (longer + more popular → right side), while PC2 (y-axis) represents the trade-off (long-but-unpopular vs. short-but-popular).
The vindication: The clear cluster separation validates our K-means groupings. The algorithm found real structure in the data, not random noise or wishful thinking. Sometimes machine learning actually works exactly as advertised. Mark this day.
Bottom Line: The songs naturally group into distinct types. It’s not random-there’s an actual pattern to what works and what doesn’t. Math proves the soundtrack is well-designed, whether or not that was intentional.



Popularity Distribution: The Full Picture


                            
                                            



Distribution Stats: The popularity distribution is relatively symmetric with mean (46.9) kissing close to median (49.0), suggesting balanced representation across the soundtrack. No extreme outliers-even the top songs stay within 2 standard deviations.
What this means: This isn’t a “one-hit wonder” album propped up by a single mega-hit while everything else languishes. It’s a soundtrack with consistent quality-the kind of depth that keeps entire albums in rotation instead of just the singles. Old-school music industry, meet your validation.
Bottom Line: Every song holds its own. You’re not fast-forwarding through filler to get to the good parts-the whole album is worth listening to. That’s increasingly rare.



Duration Distribution by Popularity Tier


                            
                                            



Tier Analysis: ANOVA on duration across popularity tiers yields F=1.76, p=0.19-not statistically significant. The violin plots confirm it visually: all tiers show similar spread and central tendency.
Translation for executives: Stop telling artists to “cut it down to 3 minutes.” High-popularity songs aren’t systematically shorter than mid or low-popularity tracks. Make it good, make it memorable, and listeners will stay for however long it takes. The data has spoken, and it’s tired of your arbitrary time limits.
Bottom Line: The “3-minute rule” is made up. Popular songs can be any length. The only rule is: don’t be boring.

title: Defying Analytics
section: Statistical Rigor: The Tests That Matter
text:
Statistical Rigor: The Tests That Matter


Correlation Analysis
Pearson Correlation (Duration vs. Popularity):
- r = 0.05, p = 0.80
- Interpretation: Essentially zero correlation. Duration explains less than 0.3% of variance in popularity (r² = 0.0025).


ANOVA: Duration Across Popularity Tiers
One-Way ANOVA:
- F-statistic = 1.76, p-value = 0.19
- Interpretation: No significant difference in mean duration across low/mid/high popularity groups. Fails to reject null hypothesis at α=0.05.


T-Test: Long vs. Short Songs
Independent Samples T-Test (median split at 3.88 min):
- t = -0.15, p = 0.88
- Interpretation: Long songs (>3.88 min) have nearly identical mean popularity (46.0) as short songs (45.8). No meaningful difference.


K-Means Clustering
Optimal Clusters: k=3 (Elbow Method + Silhouette Score)
- Cluster 0: n=8, epic showstoppers (long, popular)
- Cluster 1: n=5, international variants (moderate length, low/zero popularity)
- Cluster 2: n=15, solid mid-tier (short-to-moderate, balanced popularity)
Within-Cluster Sum of Squares: Well-separated clusters with minimal intra-cluster variance.


Principal Component Analysis
Explained Variance:
- PC1: 78.3% (captures combined duration + popularity magnitude)
- PC2: 21.7% (captures duration-popularity trade-off)
- Total: 100% variance explained with 2 components
Interpretation: The 2D projection retains all information from the original 2-feature space (duration, popularity), making it ideal for visualization without information loss.

title: Defying Analytics
section: Key Takeaways: What The Data Actually Says
text:
Key Takeaways: What The Data Actually Says


1. Duration Is a Red Herring
Every piece of conventional wisdom says “shorter songs perform better in the streaming era.” The Wicked soundtrack says: not so fast. With r=0.05 and p=0.80, there’s no statistical relationship between song length and popularity. “Dancing Through Life” (7.62 minutes) and “For Good” (5.11 minutes) both outperform most shorter tracks.
Lesson: Content quality and emotional resonance matter more than runtime. Listeners will stick with a song if it delivers—whether it’s 90 seconds or 7 minutes.


2. Three Distinct Song Archetypes
K-means clustering reveals the soundtrack serves three audiences:

Epic Showstoppers: Long, popular, memorable—the tracks people think of when they think “Wicked”
Narrative Builders: Shorter supporting tracks that advance the plot but don’t necessarily dominate playlists
International Variants: Translations and alternate versions (low Spotify presence but important for global reach)

Lesson: A successful soundtrack isn’t monolithic. It needs variety—peaks and valleys, bombast and intimacy.


3. “For Good” Defies Expectations
Nobody predicted the quiet, emotional duet would beat “Defying Gravity.” But it does (58 vs. 56). This might reflect:

Emotional depth: Listeners return to songs that make them feel, not just sing along
Replayability: “Defying Gravity” is a showstopper, but you don’t play it every day. “For Good” is a comfort song.
Under-the-radar favoritism: Not the flashiest choice, but the one that sticks

Lesson: Flashy doesn’t always equal popular. Sometimes the understated moments resonate more deeply.


4. The Data’s Blind Spots
This analysis tells us what is popular (and what isn’t), but it can’t explain why certain songs resonate. The Spotify API gives us numbers—duration, popularity scores—but it can’t capture cultural moments, emotional connections, or the ineffable magic that makes a song meaningful to listeners.
Lesson: Numbers tell you where to look. Context tells you what you’re looking at. Good data science acknowledges its limits.

text:
Technical Learnings

API Integration: Working with Spotify’s Web API taught me the importance of rate limiting, error handling, and data validation. Not every API call succeeds-building in retry logic and graceful failures is essential.
Statistical Storytelling: Raw test results (r=0.05, p=0.80) mean nothing without interpretation. The real skill is translating statistical jargon into insights a non-technical audience can understand and act on.
Visualization Choices: Interactive charts > static images. Plotly’s hover effects and zoom capabilities let users explore the data themselves, increasing engagement and understanding.
Knowing When to Stop: I could’ve added more features, more tests, more models. But at some point, you’re not adding insight-you’re just adding complexity. The best analysis is the one that answers the question clearly, not the one that throws every tool at the problem.


The Real Insight
Data science can tell you what happened. With enough data, it can even tell you how it happened. But the why-the cultural moments, the emotional connections, the reasons “For Good” resonates more than “Defying Gravity”-that requires human interpretation.
This project taught me that the best analysis acknowledges its limitations. The numbers got us 80% of the way there. The other 20%? That’s where the story lives.

Project Overview

Twenty years after its Broadway debut, Wicked remains a streaming phenomenon. But what separates the most-played tracks from the forgotten ones? I set out to answer this using real Spotify data from 28 tracks, armed with statistics and a healthy skepticism of conventional wisdom.
Spoiler alert: Almost everything the music industry tells you about “successful songs” is backwards.
Using correlation analysis, ANOVA, K-means clustering, and PCA, I analyzed actual Spotify metrics to understand what makes certain songs resonate. The plan was simple: prove that shorter songs dominate streaming, that popularity follows predictable patterns, and that “Defying Gravity” reigns supreme.
Reality had other plans.
Turns out “For Good” wins, duration doesn’t matter even slightly (r=0.05, p=0.80), and the data reveals three distinct song archetypes that nobody talks about. Sometimes the best research findings are the ones that make you rethink everything you thought you knew.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
What The Data Actually Showed

The Winner Nobody Expected (Sorry, Elphaba)
“For Good,” the emotional duet near the finale, scores highest in Spotify popularity (58/100), edging out crowd favorites like “Defying Gravity” (56) and “No Good Deed” (57). Apparently listeners prefer crying to their morning coffee over belting high notes. Who knew?


Duration Doesn’t Matter (And I Have Receipts)
Correlation between song length and popularity? A measly r=0.05 with p=0.80. Translation: whether a song runs 50 seconds or 7.6 minutes has zero predictive power for streaming success. ANOVA confirms it (F=1.76, p=0.19). The “keep it short for attention spans” advice? Statistically baseless-at least for this soundtrack.


Three Song Archetypes Nobody Talks About
K-means clustering (k=3) reveals distinct groups: Epic Numbers (long, popular showstoppers), Deep Cuts (short, less-streamed but plot-essential tracks), and Solid Mid-Tier (balanced popularity and length). It’s not a hierarchy. Each serves a different purpose. The soundtrack works because it has variety, not despite it.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
Methodology: Data Collection & Analysis


Python 3.11 Spotify API Pandas SciPy Scikit-learn Plotly

I collected data on 28 tracks from the Wicked soundtrack using Spotify’s Web API, capturing track metadata (name, duration, popularity scores) and analyzing patterns in listener engagement. The goal was simple: understand what makes certain songs succeed while others fade into the background.
The approach: descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, hypothesis testing (ANOVA, t-tests), unsupervised learning (K-means clustering, PCA), and interactive visualizations. No simulated data, no assumptions. Just real numbers from real listeners.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
The Numbers Tell a Story

Top 10 Songs by Spotify Popularity


        
        
        


                            
                                            



Observation: “For Good” takes the crown with a popularity score of 58, despite being one of the soundtrack’s longer tracks at 5.11 minutes. The emotional ballad outperforms even the showstopping “Defying Gravity” (56).
What this challenges: The assumption that “big, loud finales” are always the most popular. Sometimes the heartfelt conversation between two friends hits harder than the woman flying away on a broomstick. Data: 1, Conventional Wisdom: 0.
Bottom Line: The quiet moments win. People return to songs that make them feel something real, not just songs that make them want to sing along.



Duration vs. Popularity: The Surprising Non-Relationship


                            
                                            



Statistical Reality Check: With a correlation coefficient of just r=0.05 and p=0.80, there’s no statistically significant relationship between song duration and popularity. Duration explains less than 0.3% of variance in popularity (r²=0.0025).
What this demolishes: The entire “TL;DR generation needs 2-minute songs” narrative. “Dancing Through Life” clocks in at 7.62 minutes and sits comfortably in the top 10. Long-form content wins when it’s actually good. Revolutionary concept, I know.
Bottom Line: Song length doesn’t matter. If people love it, they’ll listen to all 7 minutes. If they don’t, they’ll skip it at 30 seconds. Quality > runtime.



K-Means Clustering: Three Song Archetypes


                            
                                            



Cluster Insight: K-means analysis (k=3) reveals three distinct song types that actually make sense:

Cluster 0: Epic Showstoppers - Long (avg 6.18 min), popular (avg 50.6), the tracks people queue up specifically
Cluster 1: International Variants - Low/zero popularity on main Spotify (foreign language versions serve different markets)
Cluster 2: Solid Mid-Tier - Shorter (avg 2.69 min), balanced popularity (avg 47.9), the narrative glue holding it all together

What this reveals: Successful soundtracks aren’t monoliths. They need peaks and valleys. The “filler tracks” aren’t filler-they’re structural. Remove them and the whole thing collapses. It’s data-driven vindication for every “I’m Not That Girl (Reprise)” out there.
Bottom Line: Great albums need variety. You can’t have all bangers-the quiet moments make the big moments matter. The “boring” tracks aren’t mistakes; they’re part of the design.



PCA Visualization: The Hidden Structure


                            
                                            



PCA Interpretation: Principal Component Analysis reduces our duration-popularity feature space to 2D while retaining 100% of the variance. PC1 (x-axis) captures combined magnitude (longer + more popular → right side), while PC2 (y-axis) represents the trade-off (long-but-unpopular vs. short-but-popular).
The vindication: The clear cluster separation validates our K-means groupings. The algorithm found real structure in the data, not random noise or wishful thinking. Sometimes machine learning actually works exactly as advertised. Mark this day.
Bottom Line: The songs naturally group into distinct types. It’s not random-there’s an actual pattern to what works and what doesn’t. Math proves the soundtrack is well-designed, whether or not that was intentional.



Popularity Distribution: The Full Picture


                            
                                            



Distribution Stats: The popularity distribution is relatively symmetric with mean (46.9) kissing close to median (49.0), suggesting balanced representation across the soundtrack. No extreme outliers-even the top songs stay within 2 standard deviations.
What this means: This isn’t a “one-hit wonder” album propped up by a single mega-hit while everything else languishes. It’s a soundtrack with consistent quality-the kind of depth that keeps entire albums in rotation instead of just the singles. Old-school music industry, meet your validation.
Bottom Line: Every song holds its own. You’re not fast-forwarding through filler to get to the good parts-the whole album is worth listening to. That’s increasingly rare.



Duration Distribution by Popularity Tier


                            
                                            



Tier Analysis: ANOVA on duration across popularity tiers yields F=1.76, p=0.19-not statistically significant. The violin plots confirm it visually: all tiers show similar spread and central tendency.
Translation for executives: Stop telling artists to “cut it down to 3 minutes.” High-popularity songs aren’t systematically shorter than mid or low-popularity tracks. Make it good, make it memorable, and listeners will stay for however long it takes. The data has spoken, and it’s tired of your arbitrary time limits.
Bottom Line: The “3-minute rule” is made up. Popular songs can be any length. The only rule is: don’t be boring.

title: Defying Analytics
section: Statistical Rigor: The Tests That Matter
text:
Statistical Rigor: The Tests That Matter


Correlation Analysis
Pearson Correlation (Duration vs. Popularity):
- r = 0.05, p = 0.80
- Interpretation: Essentially zero correlation. Duration explains less than 0.3% of variance in popularity (r² = 0.0025).


ANOVA: Duration Across Popularity Tiers
One-Way ANOVA:
- F-statistic = 1.76, p-value = 0.19
- Interpretation: No significant difference in mean duration across low/mid/high popularity groups. Fails to reject null hypothesis at α=0.05.


T-Test: Long vs. Short Songs
Independent Samples T-Test (median split at 3.88 min):
- t = -0.15, p = 0.88
- Interpretation: Long songs (>3.88 min) have nearly identical mean popularity (46.0) as short songs (45.8). No meaningful difference.


K-Means Clustering
Optimal Clusters: k=3 (Elbow Method + Silhouette Score)
- Cluster 0: n=8, epic showstoppers (long, popular)
- Cluster 1: n=5, international variants (moderate length, low/zero popularity)
- Cluster 2: n=15, solid mid-tier (short-to-moderate, balanced popularity)
Within-Cluster Sum of Squares: Well-separated clusters with minimal intra-cluster variance.


Principal Component Analysis
Explained Variance:
- PC1: 78.3% (captures combined duration + popularity magnitude)
- PC2: 21.7% (captures duration-popularity trade-off)
- Total: 100% variance explained with 2 components
Interpretation: The 2D projection retains all information from the original 2-feature space (duration, popularity), making it ideal for visualization without information loss.

title: Defying Analytics
section: Key Takeaways: What The Data Actually Says (vs. What Everyone Assumes)
text:
Key Takeaways: What The Data Actually Says (vs. What Everyone Assumes)


1. Duration Is a Red Herring (But Everyone Acts Like It Isn’t)
Every streaming era thinkpiece insists “shorter songs perform better because attention spans are dead.” The Wicked soundtrack responds: citation needed.
With r=0.05 and p=0.80, there’s no statistical relationship between song length and popularity. “Dancing Through Life” (7.62 minutes) and “For Good” (5.11 minutes) both outperform most shorter tracks. ANOVA confirms no difference across popularity tiers (F=1.76, p=0.19). T-test comparing long vs. short songs? t=-0.15, p=0.88. Statistically identical.
Real lesson: Content quality and emotional resonance matter more than runtime. Listeners will stick with a song if it delivers-whether it’s 90 seconds or 7 minutes. Stop cutting good art to fit arbitrary time limits that the data doesn’t support.


2. Three Distinct Song Archetypes (That the Industry Doesn’t Name)
K-means clustering reveals the soundtrack serves three distinct functions:

Epic Showstoppers: Long, popular, memorable-the tracks people think of when they hear “Wicked”
Narrative Builders: Shorter supporting tracks that advance plot but don’t necessarily dominate playlists
International Variants: Translations and alternate versions (low Spotify presence but crucial for global reach)

Real lesson: A successful soundtrack isn’t monolithic. It needs variety-peaks and valleys, bombast and intimacy. The “filler” tracks aren’t failures; they’re structural necessities. Remove the connective tissue and the whole body stops working.


3. “For Good” Defies Every Prediction
Nobody-and I mean nobody-predicted the quiet, emotional duet would beat “Defying Gravity.” But it does (58 vs. 56). This might reflect:

Emotional depth: Listeners return to songs that make them feel, not just sing along
Replayability: “Defying Gravity” is a showstopper, but you don’t blast it at 7 AM every Tuesday. “For Good” is a comfort song-the one you need when life gets complicated.
Under-the-radar favoritism: Not the flashiest choice, but the one that sticks in your chest

Real lesson: Flashy doesn’t always equal popular. The moments that make us cry often resonate more deeply than the ones that make us cheer. Marketing loves the big moments, but listeners love what they love-and data doesn’t lie about it.


4. The Data’s Blind Spots (And Why That’s Important)
This analysis tells us what is popular and what correlates (or doesn’t). But it can’t explain why certain songs resonate. Was “For Good” boosted by a viral moment we missed? A celebrity cover? An emotional social media trend? The CSV doesn’t capture cultural context, personal memories, or the specific moment someone first heard a song that changed them.
Real lesson: Numbers tell you where to look. Context tells you what you’re seeing. Good data science acknowledges its limits. Great data science uses those limits to ask better questions for the next project.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
Technical Learnings

API Integration: Working with Spotify’s Web API taught me the importance of rate limiting, error handling, and data validation. Not every API call succeeds-building in retry logic and graceful failures is essential.
Statistical Storytelling: Raw test results (r=0.05, p=0.80) mean nothing without interpretation. The real skill is translating statistical jargon into insights a non-technical audience can understand and act on.
Visualization Choices: Interactive charts > static images. Plotly’s hover effects and zoom capabilities let users explore the data themselves, increasing engagement and understanding.
Knowing When to Stop: I could’ve added more features, more tests, more models. But at some point, you’re not adding insight-you’re just adding complexity. The best analysis is the one that answers the question clearly, not the one that throws every tool at the problem.


The Real Insight
Data science can tell you what happened. With enough data, it can even tell you how it happened. But the why-the cultural moments, the emotional connections, the reasons “For Good” resonates more than “Defying Gravity”-that requires human interpretation.
This project taught me that the best analysis acknowledges its limitations. The numbers got us 80% of the way there. The other 20%? That’s where the story lives.

title: Defying Analytics
text:
What’s Next: Future Directions
If I were to extend this analysis or build something similar:
1. Audio Feature Deep-Dive
Spotify provides 10+ audio features (danceability, energy, valence, tempo, acousticness, etc.). Analyzing how these correlate with popularity could reveal why certain songs succeed beyond just duration.
2. Time-Series Analysis
Track how popularity scores change over time. Do songs gain popularity post-movie release? Do certain tracks spike during award season or viral moments?
3. Cross-Soundtrack Comparison
How does Wicked compare to Hamilton, Dear Evan Hansen, or Six? Are the patterns universal across Broadway soundtracks, or is each unique?
4. Sentiment Analysis
Mine YouTube comments, Reddit discussions, and social media to understand why people connect with certain songs. Qualitative data could fill in the gaps quantitative analysis misses.
5. Predictive Modeling
Build a model to predict which tracks from new musicals will become streaming hits. Won’t be perfect (nothing is), but could help marketing teams prioritize promotion.
6. Lyrical Analysis
Use NLP to analyze song lyrics-word frequency, sentiment, complexity. Do simpler lyrics correlate with higher popularity? Do emotional themes matter?
